overview: GPS fixes from vehicles are noisy (multipath, urban canyons, dropouts), so a raw track wanders off the road, onto parallel streets and across buildings. PathSnap reconstructs the road segments a vehicle actually used. For every GPS point we (1) generate candidate road arcs near it, (2) score each candidate with a supervised classifier trained on 33 engineered features, and (3) decode the most likely connected sequence of arcs with a Hidden Markov Model and the Viterbi algorithm, whose emissions are the classifier probabilities and whose transitions come from road-network connectivity. The decoded arcs are stitched into a continuous route. A FastAPI service (Laptop 1) holds the model, decoder, road networks and server-side evaluation; a Streamlit UI (Laptop 2) lets the evaluator pick one of the ten reserved trips and displays the predicted route and its metrics. Partitions: 80 train trips (fitting, cross-validation, tuning), 10 student-test trips (model comparison), 10 evaluator trips (final evaluation only, never used during development).
eda_patterns: (1) Every trip comes with its own road network from a different city or country, ranging from a few hundred to over 300 000 arcs, so the model must generalise across regions: no absolute coordinates are used as features. (2) GPS noise is small but heavy-tailed: the median distance to the reference route is about 4.5 m while the 95th percentile reaches 12-30 m in normal trips. (3) About 95 % of arcs have a reverse twin with identical geometry, which makes the nearest-arc rule fail half of the time on two-way roads (Top-1 0.54) - direction of travel is essential. (4) Sampling is nominally 1 Hz but long gaps exist (one of 42 hours), so temporal features and gap handling in the decoder are needed. (5) Some reference routes cover only part of the drive (up to 89 % of points unmatched in one trip), so labels must allow an unmatched state. (6) Networks are not fully connected, so impossible transitions must be handled explicitly. Neighbouring points are strongly correlated, which motivated the temporal context features and trip-grouped cross-validation.

logreg.why: A linear, well-calibrated probabilistic baseline: the strongest signals (distance, heading agreement, neighbour agreement) are roughly monotonic, so a linear decision function on standardised features should already separate most candidates, and its probabilities feed the HMM directly.
logreg.strengths: Fast to train (about 6 s on all 1.08 M training rows) and predict, stable across folds, interpretable coefficients, reasonable calibration (log loss 0.13). Limitation: it cannot model interactions such as distance mattering differently when heading is unreliable or when many candidates are close; it ends at the level of the hand-made distance+heading rule (CV Top-1 0.868 vs 0.868).
logreg.loss: Binary cross-entropy (log loss) with L2 regularisation, minimised by L-BFGS; StandardScaler fitted inside the pipeline on training folds only.
logreg.fit: The gap between training-fold and held-out Top-1 is small (about 1.7 pp) and student-test agrees with CV, so there is no over-fitting; the model is limited by bias (under-fitting): even on training trips it stays far below the tree ensembles (0.886 vs 0.95).

gaussian_nb.why: The simplest generative probabilistic model, included to test whether per-class feature distributions alone are enough and as an extremely cheap scorer.
gaussian_nb.strengths: Trains in about one second and predicts quickly. Limitation: the conditional-independence assumption is badly violated - d, log_d, d_minus_min, rank and the context distances all encode the same information - so evidence is counted many times, making probabilities over-confident and the decision threshold biased.
gaussian_nb.loss: Maximum-likelihood estimation of per-class Gaussian means and variances (no iterative loss); predictions via Bayes rule.
gaussian_nb.fit: Clear under-fitting: training-fold Top-1 is only 0.839 and log loss is about 0.90 even on training trips. Precision on the positive class is only 0.56 with recall 0.92 - the model flags far too many candidates as correct - and fold variability is the highest of all models (std 0.067).

knn.why: An instance-based method: if a (point, candidate) pair looks like stored training pairs in feature space, it should share their label; no parametric form is assumed.
knn.strengths: Non-parametric and simple; distance weighting gives smooth probabilities. Limitations: prediction cost grows with the stored reference set (684 ms per 1000 GPS points, about 120x slower than XGBoost), so the reference set had to be sub-sampled to 20 000 observations; all 33 standardised features weigh equally in the Euclidean distance although only a few are informative.
knn.loss: No training loss: the 25 nearest stored rows (Euclidean distance on standardised features) vote with weights 1/distance.
knn.fit: Training-fold Top-1 0.891 vs CV 0.864 vs student-test 0.862: a modest gap and no over-fitting thanks to k = 25 and distance weighting, but the model under-fits relative to the tree ensembles because of the sub-sampled reference set and the uninformative dimensions diluting the metric.

random_forest.why: Bagged decision trees capture non-linear interactions (for example heading only matters when the vehicle moves) without feature scaling, and averaging many trees reduces variance.
random_forest.strengths: Strong accuracy (CV Top-1 0.887), robust to outliers and correlated features, little tuning needed. Limitations: largest model and slowest to train among the ensembles (94 s for 150 trees), inference 22 ms per 1000 points, and deep trees memorise training trips.
random_forest.loss: Each tree greedily minimises Gini impurity; probabilities are the average of leaf class frequencies over 150 bootstrap trees.
random_forest.fit: Highest variance of all models: Top-1 0.972 on training-fold trips vs 0.887 held out (8.5 pp gap) and log loss 0.040 vs 0.095 - the trees fit the training trips almost perfectly. Bagging keeps the held-out score high, so this is benign over-fitting rather than harmful, but it is why boosting with shallower trees generalises slightly better.

hist_gb.why: Gradient boosting builds an additive model of shallow trees, each correcting the previous errors - a strong default for tabular data with mixed-scale features; the histogram implementation keeps training fast on a million rows.
hist_gb.strengths: Good accuracy (student-test Top-1 0.890) at a moderate cost (15 s fit). Limitations: with 300 iterations at learning rate 0.1 and no early stopping its probabilities are less well calibrated than XGBoost/LightGBM (log loss 0.097 vs 0.082) and continuity of its raw predictions is lowest among the boosters.
hist_gb.loss: Binary cross-entropy (log loss) minimised by gradient boosting with second-order (Newton) leaf values.
hist_gb.fit: Training-fold Top-1 0.935 vs CV 0.882 vs student-test 0.890: moderate, expected gap; student-test is in line with CV, so no harmful over-fitting.

lightgbm.why: Leaf-wise gradient boosting with row and column sub-sampling: efficient on 1 M rows, models feature interactions and produces well-calibrated probabilities, which the HMM needs.
lightgbm.strengths: Best CV Top-1 (0.889) and CV macro-F1 among boosters, fast training (18 s). Limitations: leaf-wise growth with 63 leaves can over-fit small data; inference (22 ms per 1000 points) was about 4x slower than XGBoost in our runs.
lightgbm.loss: Binary cross-entropy (log loss) with L2 regularisation (reg_lambda = 1), gradient-boosted with learning rate 0.05.
lightgbm.fit: Training-fold Top-1 0.952 vs CV 0.889 vs student-test 0.891. The real training history (Figure 15b) shows the student-test log loss flattening at about 0.085 after roughly 120 iterations while the training loss keeps falling to 0.06 - mild over-fitting in the later iterations, but the held-out loss never rises, so performance is not degraded.

xgboost.why: Regularised gradient boosting with depth-limited trees and a histogram split finder: captures the non-linear interactions between distance, heading and neighbour context, regularises strongly, and is fast at inference.
xgboost.strengths: Best student-test Top-1 (0.899), macro-F1 (0.937) and log loss (0.082) and the fastest boosted model at inference (about 6 ms per 1000 points). Limitations: many interacting hyperparameters (depth, learning rate, regularisation, sampling), which motivates Bayesian optimisation; still a per-point model, so route continuity of raw predictions is only about 0.81.
xgboost.loss: Binary cross-entropy (logistic loss) plus L2 regularisation on leaf weights, optimised with second-order gradient boosting (learning rate 0.05, 400 trees, max depth 7).
xgboost.fit: Training-fold Top-1 0.950 vs CV 0.888 vs student-test 0.899. The per-iteration history (Figure 15a) shows the student-test log loss plateauing at about 0.083 after roughly 150 iterations while the training loss keeps decreasing (0.063 at 400), so the later trees mostly fit the training trips (mild over-fitting); the held-out loss never increases, and CV and student-test agree within 1 pp, so generalisation is not harmed. The number of trees and the regularisation strength are therefore natural targets for tuning.

mlp.why: A feed-forward neural network can learn arbitrary non-linear combinations of the features and gives smooth probabilities; it represents the neural-network family.
mlp.strengths: Competitive student-test Top-1 (0.892) and very fast inference (3 ms per 1000 points). Limitations: slowest to train (about 200 s on 80 000 observations with early stopping), sensitive to scaling and initialisation, and higher fold variability (std 0.044) than the boosters.
mlp.loss: Binary cross-entropy minimised by Adam (learning rate 0.001, batch 512, L2 alpha 1e-4), early stopping on a 10 % validation split (patience 6 epochs).
mlp.fit: Training-fold Top-1 0.917 vs CV 0.881 vs student-test 0.892. sklearn's built-in history (Figure 15c) only records validation accuracy on a random 10 % of rows, so we additionally trained the same network epoch by epoch on a trip-grouped split (scripts/03b_mlp_loss_curve.py, Figure 15d: 64 training trips vs 16 held-out trips): the held-out log loss stops improving after epoch 8 (best 0.112) and then fluctuates between 0.113 and 0.119 while the training loss keeps falling from 0.083 to 0.078 - a clear sign of over-fitting beyond about 8 epochs, which early stopping on the held-out loss prevents. The remaining gap to boosting is due to the sub-sampled training set and the higher variance of the network.

selection: XGBoost and LightGBM are tied on the primary metric (CV Top-1 0.888 vs 0.889, well within the fold standard deviation of about 0.04, which reflects how hard individual trips are rather than model differences). XGBoost was selected because (a) it is best on every student-test metric - Top-1 0.899, macro-F1 0.937, log loss 0.082 - so its probabilities are the best input for the HMM, (b) it was about 4x faster at inference than LightGBM, which matters for the API, (c) its training history shows no harmful over-fitting. Random Forest has similar accuracy but over-fits the training trips the most and is slower; logistic regression, KNN and Gaussian NB are clearly worse; the MLP is competitive but less stable across folds and much slower to train. All learned ensembles beat the hand-made distance+heading rule by 2-4 pp of Top-1, and every model beats the nearest-arc baseline by more than 25 pp.
bayes_discussion: Did the tuned model outperform the untuned one? On the optimised objective, yes, but only slightly: CV Top-1 rose from 0.8879 to 0.8907 (+0.28 pp) and CV macro-F1 from 0.9301 to 0.9312. All 23 completed trials lie between 0.881 and 0.891 (std 0.0025), i.e. XGBoost is not very sensitive to its hyperparameters on this data - the features carry most of the signal - and the gain is smaller than the fold-to-fold standard deviation (about 0.037). As a stand-alone classifier the tuned model was not better on student-test: Top-1 0.8944 vs 0.8992, log loss 0.087 vs 0.082 (CV log loss also worse, 0.100 vs 0.094), and inference is about 4.5x slower (800 trees of depth 11 vs 400 of depth 7). The main reason is scale_pos_weight = 2.31: up-weighting the positive class optimises the ranking used by Top-1 but shifts probabilities upwards, which costs calibration (log loss). Because the deployed system is classifier + HMM, we decided between the two models with a leakage-free test on the training data: the HMM decoder was tuned and evaluated on the out-of-fold probabilities of each model (scripts/05_hmm_eval.py, untuned results kept in results/hmm_untuned/). Train-OOF Top-1 after HMM was 0.9361 (tuned) vs 0.9360 (untuned) - a tie, slightly in favour of the tuned model - and on student-test the tuned model + HMM reached 0.9513 vs 0.9383. The tuned model's less extreme probabilities on wrong-but-close candidates give the decoder more room to correct them, so the tuned XGBoost is the deployed model. Evaluator data was never used for any of these decisions. Computational cost: 30 trials in 95 min of wall time on a 22-thread laptop CPU (median-pruning stopped 7 unpromising trials early); refitting the tuned model on all train rows takes 50 s.

hmm.states: At GPS observation t the hidden state is one of its candidate arcs (at most 8 within 50 m, plus ties), stored together with the projection of the GPS point on that arc (fractional position u). Rows of the candidate table are kept in the same order as the classifier input, so every state maps one-to-one to an arc id and a classifier probability (candidate-to-road-segment correspondence is preserved).
hmm.emission: log P(o_t | c) = w_e * log p_c, where p_c is the selected classifier's probability that c is the true arc, re-normalised over the candidates of observation t (floor 1e-6). Because the classifier already uses distance, heading and context, it acts as a learned emission model; w_e balances emission against transition evidence.
hmm.transition: Following Newson and Krumm, a correct transition is one where the distance driven along the network between the two projected positions is close to the straight-line distance between the two GPS fixes: log P(a -> b) = -(|d_net - d_gc| + U-turn penalty) / beta. d_net is computed exactly: same arc forward = (u_b - u_a) x length; different arcs = rest of arc a + shortest path from the end node of a to the start node of b (bounded Dijkstra, limit max(250 m, 3 d_gc + 50 m)) + the part of b before the projection. Moving onto the reverse twin or backwards on the same arc adds uturn_m metres. Unreachable pairs get probability zero.
hmm.viterbi: delta_t(b) = log P(o_t | b) + max_a [ delta_{t-1}(a) + log P(a -> b) ], with back-pointers psi_t(b) = argmax_a. The recurrence is vectorised as a (k_{t-1} x k_t) matrix per step in log space; the best final state is traced back through psi. Network distances are pre-computed once per trip (cached Dijkstra per source node), so decoding with other parameters is cheap.
hmm.gaps: A point without candidates (no arc within 200 m after radius expansion) gets no state: the current chain is decoded and closed, the point is left unassigned (counted as an error in strict accuracy) and a new chain starts at the next point. If the time gap to the previous fix exceeds gap_s, the chain is also broken and restarted from the emission probabilities, because the network distance between fixes far apart in time is not informative.
hmm.disconnected: If every transition from the previous observation is impossible (no path within the search limit - e.g. disconnected network components or a GPS jump), the current chain is decoded up to t-1 and a new chain starts at t, so decoding never fails. When the decoded arcs of consecutive points are not directly adjacent, the route-stitching step inserts the shortest connecting path (up to 3 km); if none exists the gap is counted as unbridged.

hmm_discussion: Effect of HMM decoding. With the tuned classifier, HMM/Viterbi raised student-test Top-1 from 0.8944 to 0.9513 (+5.7 pp) and train-OOF Top-1 from 0.8896 to 0.9361 (+4.7 pp). Route quality improves even more: plausible continuity rises from 0.83 to 0.99 (student-test) and from 0.75 to 0.98 (train), the number of unbridged gaps in the stitched route drops from 72 to 3 (student-test) and from 1015 to 64 (train), and route F1 rises from 0.81 to 0.96 because the classifier-only route contains many spurious arcs (route precision 0.69 -> 0.93) while recall was already high. Tuning the decoder on train-OOF probabilities gave beta = 3 m, U-turn penalty 25 m, emission weight 0.5 and gap threshold 60 s; it adds 1.4 pp over the hand-picked defaults on student-test (0.9369 -> 0.9513) and 0.75 pp on train OOF. The best settings use a small beta and an emission weight below 1, i.e. the network-distance evidence should dominate the per-point classifier when they disagree. Direct continuity stays at 0.89 because consecutive 1 Hz points often skip very short arcs (the next arc is reached through an intermediate one); these gaps are legitimate and are filled by stitching. Where HMM did not help. On 9 of 10 student-test trips the HMM improved Top-1 (largest gain +16.9 pp on trip 00000077). It hurt trip 00000065 (-3.5 pp): the errors concentrate on a divided road whose two one-way carriageways run a few metres apart (Section 6) - once the chain enters the wrong carriageway, connectivity keeps it there for the whole stretch. On train the clearest failure is trip 00000010 (Top-1 0.683 -> 0.551): it is slow (median 8.4 m/s, 12.9 GPS points per route arc), has an unusually high share of one-way arcs (two-way fraction 0.82 vs a median of 0.95) and the classifier alone was already poor (route F1 0.37). The HMM enforced a consistent route that partly followed the wrong parallel road - Top-1 fell but route F1 still improved from 0.37 to 0.69. Gaps and disconnections are handled gracefully: 6 chain breaks on student-test (time gaps above 60 s or no feasible transition) and 516 on train (mostly the long gaps and partial-route trips found in the EDA).
maps_discussion: On the best trip (00000007, Top-1 99.8 %) the HMM route coincides with the reference and only 3 GPS points are assigned to a different arc. On the median trip (00000076, 97.0 %) the 45 wrong points cluster at the turns and junctions of the route, where the vehicle passes from one arc to the next and the derived label itself is least certain. On the worst trip (00000065, 87.8 %) the wrong points form one continuous run along a divided road: the predicted route follows the parallel carriageway for that stretch - the failure mode discussed in Section 5. Switching on the orange classifier-only layer in the HTML maps shows its fragmented, disconnected arcs, which the HMM replaces by a single connected route.
deploy: Laptop 1 runs the FastAPI service (api/main.py, uvicorn on 0.0.0.0:8000). At start-up it loads the exported artifacts (artifacts/model.joblib, feature_cols.json, candidate_params.json, hmm_params.json, model_card.json) and lists the trips in PATHSNAP_TRIPS_DIR (default data/eval). For POST /predict it runs the full pipeline (src/pathsnap/pipeline.py): load and clean the track, project, generate candidates, build features, classify, decode with HMM/Viterbi and stitch the route. Only afterwards is the .route file read, server-side, to compute metrics; the response contains only aggregate metrics, never the reference route or labels. Every request is logged to the console and logs/api.log (client IP, trip, number of points and candidates, per-stage timings, metrics). Laptop 2 runs the Streamlit UI (ui/app.py), which only talks to the API: it shows the trips returned by /trips, sends the selected trip id, and draws the GPS points and predicted route on a Folium map with layer control and legend, plus the metrics and timings. Both laptops must be on the same network; the API port (8000) must be allowed through the Windows firewall on Laptop 1.
conclusion: PathSnap reconstructs vehicle routes with an end-to-end pipeline that runs in about 1 s per student-test trip: candidate arcs within 50 m (miss rate 0.22 % on student-test), an Optuna-tuned XGBoost classifier on 33 location-independent features (student-test Top-1 0.894 alone) and HMM/Viterbi decoding using road-network distances, which raises Top-1 to 0.951, plausible continuity to 0.99 and route F1 to 0.96. The comparison of eight models showed that gradient-boosted trees capture the interactions between distance, direction of travel and neighbouring-point context best, that the direction of travel is essential on two-way roads, and that sequential decoding contributes more than hyperparameter tuning. Limitations. (1) Per-point labels are derived from the reference route by our alignment and inherit its errors; points at junctions are inherently ambiguous and trips whose reference route covers only part of the drive were partly excluded. (2) Arcs are straight segments between nodes; curved roads without intermediate nodes have larger apparent GPS errors. (3) Parallel one-way carriageways a few metres apart remain the main failure mode, for both the classifier and the HMM. (4) Bayesian optimisation used 30 trials and improved CV Top-1 only marginally; the tuned model is slower and slightly less calibrated as a stand-alone classifier. (5) The student-test set has only 10 trips, so differences below about 1 pp between models are not significant. Possible improvements: a carriageway-aware feature (side of the road relative to the direction of travel), probability calibration before decoding, and learning the transition model from data.
